label: Jacobi Fields
notes: This chapter, printed pages 110 through 123, introduces the variational machinery that measures how nearby geodesics drift apart. A Jacobi field records the infinitesimal velocity of a one-parameter family of geodesics, and it obeys a second-order linear equation governed entirely by the curvature tensor of the manifold.

label: Variations of Geodesics
notes: We begin with a smooth family of curves sharing a base geodesic. The variation field is the transverse derivative of this family at the base parameter. When every curve in the family is itself a geodesic, the variation field is forced to satisfy a distinguished differential equation derived below.

label: The Jacobi Equation
notes: Differentiating the geodesic equation across the family and applying the symmetry of mixed covariant derivatives produces the Jacobi equation. The curvature term appears because the order of covariant differentiation in the transverse and tangential directions differs precisely by the Riemann tensor acting on the variation field.

label: Linearization of the Geodesic Flow
notes: The Jacobi equation is exactly the linearization of the nonlinear geodesic equation about a fixed geodesic. Solutions live in the tangent space along the curve, so the field decomposes into a tangential part that is affine in the parameter and a normal part that carries all the curvature information.

label: Existence and Initial Data
notes: Because the Jacobi equation is linear of second order, a Jacobi field along a geodesic is uniquely determined by its initial value and the initial value of its covariant derivative. The space of Jacobi fields therefore has dimension twice that of the manifold, a fact used repeatedly in later arguments.

label: Jacobi Fields from the Exponential Map
notes: Fixing the base point and varying only the initial velocity yields a Jacobi field vanishing at the origin. Its value at parameter one equals the differential of the exponential map applied to a tangent vector, so Jacobi fields are the concrete derivative of the exponential map along radial geodesics.

label: Conjugate Points
notes: A point is conjugate to the base point along a geodesic when a nontrivial Jacobi field vanishes at both endpoints. Equivalently the differential of the exponential map becomes singular there, so radial geodesics that started apart are refocused, signalling the failure of the exponential map to be a local diffeomorphism.

label: Multiplicity of Conjugate Points
notes: The multiplicity of a conjugate point is the dimension of the space of Jacobi fields vanishing at both endpoints, equivalently the dimension of the kernel of the exponential differential. This integer is finite and counts how many independent directions of geodesics refocus simultaneously at the conjugate point.

label: Curvature Controls Spreading
notes: For a normal Jacobi field its second covariant derivative equals minus curvature times the field. Negative curvature forces convex growth so geodesics diverge exponentially, while positive curvature acts like a restoring force, bending neighbours back together and producing conjugate points within bounded distance.

label: Conjugate Points on the Sphere
notes: On the unit sphere every great circle leaving a pole refocuses exactly at the antipode. The Jacobi field grows like the sine of the parameter, vanishing again after distance pi, so the antipode is conjugate to the pole with multiplicity equal to the dimension of the sphere minus one.

label: Index Form Preview
notes: The Jacobi equation is the Euler-Lagrange equation of the second variation of arc length, whose bilinear index form measures the stability of a geodesic. Conjugate points mark where this index form loses positive definiteness, which is the bridge to the comparison and Morse index theorems of later chapters.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We summarized Jacobi fields as linearized geodesic variations obeying a curvature-driven second order equation, identified them with the derivative of the exponential map, and characterized conjugate points by their vanishing. These tools open the comparison theory linking curvature bounds to global geometric and topological conclusions.
